text: Helen crossed the Channel, took an afternoon train toward the old battlefields, and stayed at a small hotel not three kilometers from Hagenzeele, planning to visit the cemetery the following morning. <break time="0.8s" /> In the office where visitors registered, a woman from Lancashire was weeping because she could not find the grave of her son, who had enlisted under a different name. <break time="0.8s" /> She insisted that he had died at Dickiebush, yet only the day before, as an officers wife later pointed out, she had named an entirely different place. <break time="0.8s" /> She was so overcome by grief and confusion that she finally collapsed, and the people around her had to help her onto a cot. <break time="0.8s" /> During the journey Helen had also met Missus Scarsworth, a talkative woman who visited the battlefields to photograph graves for families who could not come themselves. <break time="0.8s" /> Later, however, Missus Scarsworth confessed to Helen that one of those graves belonged to a man who had been more to her than anything in the world. <break time="0.8s" /> Tired of pretending, she admitted that her trips for others were merely a cover, and that she had already visited his grave eight times. <break time="0.8s" /> Helen could only take her hands and murmur, Oh, my dear, My dear, but Missus Scarsworth, offended, asked sharply, Is that how you take it.
